deep_why: The core decision being modeled is whether to suppress the Buy Box—the featured seller slot that drives 98% of Amazon sales. The mechanism works through visibility loss: when Amazon removes the box, search rank and ad placement disappear immediately, creating tangible economic consequences for sellers. This principle holds because sellers watch these signals closely; a 12% sales rank drop within 48 hours sends clear enforcement, teaching sellers that certain behaviors (like raising prices uncompetitively) trigger suppression. The real problem this solves is understanding how platforms govern seller behavior not through rules alone but through algorithmic visibility, which can either level or distort competition across marketplaces.

The paper exploits how safety checks scan local context by *distributing harmful intent across space* rather than hiding it in obfuscation. Safety filters typically match patterns within windows of text; when a malicious request is scattered across distant positions in a long context, the model processes pieces separately before later reconstructing intent. This works because the model's internal reasoning reassembles the fragments after passing the gated defense layer. The big problem tackled is exposing that spatial decomposition is a genuine blind spot in current safety mechanisms, motivating new detection methods that track long-range coherence of harmful directives.

Octopus solves the perception fusion problem by *consolidating sensor data at roadside hubs* instead of requiring every vehicle to communicate with every other. The principle is that one central computation that sees all observations avoids redundant communication and can refine a global picture once, then broadcast rich context back to all vehicles as priors. Why this works: each vehicle's raw sensor data is asymmetric (different viewing angles, occlusions); fusing at a hub exploits all data once to build a shared understanding. The real-world benefit is making autonomous driving real-time and network-efficient by solving the fusion problem in one place at scale rather than many-to-many chatter.

Converting unstructured text to structured knowledge graphs enables machines to reason over content systematically by *representing entities, relations, events as discrete facts with connections*. The principle is that once content is structured, downstream systems—search, reasoning, language model retrieval—can operate deterministically over facts rather than probabilistically over raw text. This works because discrete structure makes consequences explicit: if entity A relates to entity B via a specific relation, that link is queryable and verifiable. The broader problem is that vast web knowledge (papers, documents, social posts) remains hidden in unstructured text; extraction unlocks it for intelligent applications.

R2NS teaches recommendation models to distinguish items by *scheduling hard negative samples dynamically* rather than sampling randomly or from a small local subset. The core principle is curriculum learning: start with easy negatives during warm-up so the model learns basics, then gradually introduce harder negatives from the full item space as capacity grows. This works because hard negatives early crash training (the model can't distinguish anything), but once fundamentals are set, global negatives (not just popular items) provide true contrastive signal that teaches fine-grained preference. The real benefit is that this scheduling produces more robust models that generalize to rare items and avoid overfitting to frequent ones.

Multi-modal entity alignment *computes alignment scores at multiple levels*—within single modalities (text-to-text, image-to-image) and across modalities—then fuses these scores as independent decisions. The principle is that each modality reveals different facets of an entity; scoring pairs within each modality preserves modal specifics, and combining scores lets disagreement signal misalignment. This works because an entity that looks similar in images but different in text might be a false match; detecting this disagreement requires separate judgments per modality. The problem it solves is robust entity linking when entities are described by diverse information types (images, descriptions, metadata from different sources).

Early fairness prediction works by observing that fairness metrics *exhibit stable, predictable trajectories during training*. The principle is that a model's tendency toward bias or balanced performance emerges quickly and persists; if early-stage fairness correlates with final fairness, one can forecast outcomes before completion. This works because the model's capacity to overfit or underfit (the root of many fairness failures) is determined by the architecture and data early, not just at the end. By detecting unfair trajectories within 26% of training time, developers can halt runs and iterate, saving 73% of compute. The real problem is that fairness auditing currently wastes computation on training runs that will fail; early stopping brings accountability into the development cycle.

Orchestration-free service automation *extracts procedural knowledge directly from past conversations* using flowcharts and small local models. The principle is that service dialogues encode the logic and decision paths; abstracting this into flowcharts avoids hand-coding rules and enables generalization across tasks. This works because conversations are rich in procedural signals: what information is requested, which branches lead where, how exceptions are handled. By distilling this knowledge into flowcharts and training small models locally, the system avoids expensive multi-turn orchestration and privacy risks of centralized processing. The real-world benefit is privacy-preserving automation that adapts to new tasks by learning from dialogues rather than custom programming.

BeyondFacts'26 bridges computational and social science methods for analyzing online discourse by *combining NLP techniques with domain expertise* to identify and evaluate claims, arguments, and rhetorical strategies. The principle is that claims and arguments have structure that machines can detect (linguistic markers, logical form, evidentiary chains) but that structure's relevance to real-world debates requires social science grounding. This works because misinformation often succeeds through rhetorical rather than logical means; understanding persuasion requires both computational scale and conceptual rigor. The bigger problem is that echo chambers and bias grow because individual claims are analyzed without context; systematic, interdisciplinary analysis reveals patterns no single field can see alone.

Bot detection via simplicial message passing *captures group coordination patterns* that pairwise graph methods miss by modeling higher-order structures (simplexes derived from network topology). The principle is that bots often coordinate as groups, leaving footprints in patterns beyond two-node interactions: three or more bots acting in sync create higher-order signals. Weighting relations per user (user-specific cross-relation attention) further reveals bot-specific patterns because bots concentrate in certain relation types. This works because coordinated behavior requires simultaneous actions across multiple connections; bots can fake individual relationships but not fake their entire relational fingerprint when examined at multiple scales. The real benefit is detecting sophisticated bots that mimic humans in pairwise connections but fail to hide group synchronization.

Credit-power co-evolution models *forecast consumption and credit risk jointly* by capturing their bidirectional feedback loop through dynamic graph learning. The principle is that credit and energy are coupled: credit downgrade signals financial distress, which manifests in reduced power consumption; conversely, energy anomalies (sudden drops or spikes) can predict payment defaults. This works because neither signal alone is sufficient—a power drop might be maintenance, or it might signal crisis; credit risk alone can't forecast spending behavior. By modeling the feedback path explicitly (credit changes influence financing, which shifts energy use; energy anomalies become early warning), the system produces better forecasts of both. The real problem is that enterprises face hidden risk; unified modeling of coupled domains reveals vulnerabilities that single-domain methods miss.

Transparent RAG systems show *retrieval sources and reasoning steps* so users see how answers are built from knowledge, not treated as oracle truth. The principle is that transparency builds trust by making systems accountable and helps learners evaluate claims independently rather than accept them on faith. This works because disclosing sources lets users verify credibility (Is this source reputable? Is it relevant to the question?) and showing retrieval steps teaches how knowledge systems work (Which documents matched? How did the model rank them?). The big-picture problem is that RAG risks becoming a black box that amplifies whatever sources it retrieves; transparency transforms it into an educational tool that balances assistance with autonomy.

Gaussian box embeddings model hierarchical asymmetry and ambiguity by *representing concepts as boxes in geometric space, parameterized by multivariate Gaussians*. The principle is that containment (child is in parent, not vice versa) is naturally asymmetric, and boxes preserve this; Gaussian parameterization adds uncertainty to handle semantic fuzziness and polysemy (words with multiple meanings). This works because taxonomy relationships are fundamentally asymmetric—"dog" is contained in "animal", not the reverse—and points cannot express this; boxes do. The uncertainty (covariance) lets edge concepts blur; for instance, "sports" might partially overlap "entertainment." The real problem is automatic taxonomy expansion without hand-curation; proper geometry respects linguistic structure and unlocks scalable expansion.

Zero-shot claim extraction aligns with expert values by *prompting language models with expert-derived dimensions* that encode which claims fact-checkers prioritize (specificity, verifiability, scope, relevance). The principle is that expert annotations reveal what makes a claim worth checking; encoding these dimensions in prompts steers the model's output toward expert-aligned selections. This works because expert preferences are learnable from annotation patterns—which claims get selected, which rejected—and these patterns can be abstracted into checkable properties. By evaluating extracted claims against these same dimensions (using an LLM-based assessor), the system quantifies alignment with expert judgment. The real problem is that manual claim extraction doesn't scale; zero-shot scaling of expert norms enables fact-checking at web scale.

Comparing rhetoric in fact-checks *quantifies persuasion techniques* across professional and crowd-sourced sources to reveal systematic institutional differences. The principle is that communities and institutions develop distinct rhetorical norms; analyzing technique prevalence (loaded language, emotional appeals, evidence framing) uncovers what each values. This works because rhetoric shapes persuasiveness—the same false claim debunked with anger versus humor reaches different audiences—so understanding which techniques each source employs reveals their implicit theories of persuasion. Measuring crowd ratings of helpfulness alongside technique prevalence shows whether audiences reward or punish particular rhetorical means, grounding the analysis in actual impact. The broader problem is understanding whether crowdsourced fact-checking differs fundamentally from professional work; systematic rhetoric analysis makes these differences visible.
